                                  Current Midterm Subjective

1-Cell membrane permeability (2 times)
Selective Permeability
• Structural features of plasma membrane (PM) confer it with selective permeability.
• PM regulates movement of substances across it.
• Fundamental to the functioning of living cells and maintenance of intracellular physiological
conditions.
Membrane Permeability For Various Substances
• Varies greatly with type and size of molecules.
Non-Polar, Lipid-Soluble Substances
• Cross passively by dissolving in the lipid bilayer of membrane.
• Rate of penetration depends on lipid solubility and size of molecules.
Polar Substances & Ions
• Have difficulty in passing through because of the hydrophobic interior of lipid bilayer.
Macromolecules
• Cannot cross plasma membrane due to size.

2-Membrane flux
• “The amount of solute that passes through a unit area of membrane every second in one
direction”.
• If a solute occurs on both sides of a membrane, it exhibits a flux in each direction.
• Flux in one direction is independent of the flux in opposite direction.
• If influx and efflux are equal, net flux is zero.
• If flux is greater in one direction, then net flux is the difference between the two fluxes.
3-What are steroid hormones? How are these prepared? (7 times)
• Steroid hormones are synthesized from cholesterol.
• They consist of four fused carbon rings including three cyclohexyl rings and one cyclopentyl
ring combined into a single structure.
• Examples: hormones of adrenal cortex (cortisol and aldosterone) hormones of ovaries
(estrogen and progesterone) and hormone of testes (testosterone).
4-Differentiate between protein/peptide and amine hormones. (6 times)
Peptide and Protein Hormones
• Composed of amino acids.
• They include very small peptides as well as large protein molecules.
• e.g. thyrotropin-releasing hormone, TRH, has only 3 amino acids and GH and prolactin with
almost 200 amino acids.
Amine Hormones
• They are small molecules synthesized from a single amino acid tyrosine.
• They include:
• Epinephrine
• Norepinephrine
• Thyroxine
• Triiodothyronine
5-What is sarcomere?
• The arrangement of thick and thin filaments creates a pattern of repeating light and dark
bands.
• This pattern gives a striped appearance to the muscle cell.

• Each repeating unit is called a sarcomere and is the basic functional contractile unit of the
muscle.
• Each dark band in the sarcomere is called A band.
• It is anisotropic i.e. it polarizes visible light.
• It has a lighter stripe in its center called H-zone.
• H-zone is bisected by a dark line called M-line.
6- Properties of hormones (12 times)
• They act only on specific target cells or tissues.
• Hormonal action depend on the type of receptor.
• A hormone comes into contact with all tissues in the body during transport through blood,
however, only the cells containing specific receptors are affected by it.
• The action of a hormone depends on the nature of enzyme cascade linked to the receptor.
• It also depends on the effector molecules expressed in a tissue.
• For these reasons, a hormone can act on two or more different types of tissues and generate
different types of responses.
• Hormones are active at very low concentration.
• The amount of hormone produced by an endocrine gland is small.
• It is further diluted in the blood and interstitial fluid.
• The available conc. for the target cell lies between 10-8 to 10-12 M and the hormone is still
effective.
7- Nissl's bodies (2 times)
• Consist of a group of ribosomes and rough endoplasmic reticulum
• Are associated with protein synthesis
8-Cardiac muscles
• Found only in the heart.
• Striated muscles
• Share many characteristics with
skeletal muscle but differ in several important ways.
• Cardiac muscle cells (myocyte) are mononucleate.
• Skeletal muscle cells are multinucleate.
• Cardiac fibers innervated only diffusely by both:

• Excitatory sympathetic neurons
• Inhibitory parasympathetic neurons
• Skeletal muscle fibers are individually innervated by an excitatory motor axon.
• Cardiac neural innervations are modulatory only.
• Contractions are induced by electrical activity of pacemaker.
• They don’t produce discrete PSP.
• They only increase or decrease the strength of myogenic contractions.
• Cardiac muscle cells are connected electrically by intercalated disks.
• AP initiated in the pacemaker region spreads rapidly from cell to cell, through fast-conducting
pathways to all muscle cells.
9- Release of neurotransmitters
• APs in presynaptic neuron cause release of neurotrans-mitter molecules at axon terminals.
• Release occurs by exocytosis into the synaptic cleft through specialized sites on the
membrane.
10- Neurotransmitters and its types (3 times)
Amino Acids:Simple organic compounds that act as neurotransmitters.
Examples:
   - Glutamate:Primary excitatory neurotransmitter.
   - GABA:Primary inhibitory neurotransmitter.
Monoamines:Derived from amino acids, affecting mood, arousal, and emotion.
Examples:
   - Dopamine: Involved in motivation and reward.
   - Serotonin: Regulates mood, appetite, and sleep.
Acetylcholine: Involved in muscle activation, memory, and learning.
Examples:
   - Acetylcholine: Role in muscle contraction.
   - Nicotine: Binds to acetylcholine receptors.
Neuropeptides:Larger molecules that act as neurotransmitters or neuromodulators.
Examples:
   - Substance P: Involved in pain perception.

   - Endorphins: Natural painkillers and mood enhancers.
Purines: Neurotransmitters derived from ATP.
Examples:
   -Adenosine: Regulates sleep and arousal.
   - ATP: Acts as a neurotransmitter in some pathways.

unequally distributed between the two compartments”.

1= Negative Feedback:(Negative feedback is a regulatory mechanism in which a 'stimulus'
causes an opposite 'output' in order to maintain an ideal level of whatever is being regulated.)
2= Positive Feedback: Positive feedback is the amplification of a body's response to a
stimulus.

Three Components of a Single Muscle Twitch: 1= Latent period, or lag phase 2= Contraction

that is similar to the smooth endoplasmic reticulum in other cells. The main function of the SR is
to store calcium ions (Ca2+).

Acclimation refers to a physiological change in an individual stimulated by exposure to a
different, often stressful, environment. As such it represents physiological phenotypic plasticity.

condition is called rigor mortis.

1= Ca2+ ions play a crucial role in regulating the contractile activity of muscles.
2= Calcium helps to expose the active sites of actin that bind myosin heads to form cross-

Question:

Describe the normal range of hemoglobin levels for different age groups and genders.Why
do these ranges vary?

Solution:

Hemoglobin levels refer to the concentration of hemoglobin, a protein in red blood cells (RBCs),
measured in grams per deciliter (g/dL) of blood. Hemoglobin is essential for transporting oxygen from the
lungs to the tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues back to the lungs for exhalation.

Normal Hemoglobin Ranges

Infants and Children

  ● Newborns (0-1 week): 14-24 g/dL
  ● Infants (2-6 months): 9.5-13 g/dL
  ● Children (6 months-5 years): 11-14 g/dL
  ● Children (6-12 years): 11.5-15.5 g/dL

Adolescents and Adults

  ● Adolescent males (13-19 years): 13-16 g/dL
  ● Adolescent females (13-19 years): 12-16 g/dL
  ● Adult males: 13.5-17.5 g/dL
  ● Adult females: 12-16 g/dL
  ● Pregnant women: 11-14 g/dL

Variations in Hemoglobin Ranges

Hemoglobin levels can fluctuate throughout life due to various factors. Understanding these variations is
crucial for accurate diagnosis and treatment of blood disorders.

1. Age-Related Variations

Hemoglobin levels change significantly throughout life:

  ● Newborns (0-1 week):Higher hemoglobin levels (14-24 g/dL) due to fetal hemoglobin.
  ● Infants (2-6 months):Lower hemoglobin levels (9.5-13 g/dL) due to developmental changes.
  ● Children (6 months-5 years): Hemoglobin levels gradually increase (11-14 g/dL).
  ● Children (6-12 years): Hemoglobin levels continue to rise (11.5-15.5 g/dL).
  ● Adolescents and adults: Hemoglobin levels stabilize, with adult males generally having higher levels
    than females.

2. Sex-Related Variations

Adult males typically have higher hemoglobin levels than females:

  ● Adult males: 13.5-17.5 g/dL
  ● Adult females: 12-16 g/d
  ● Pregnant women: 11-14 g/dL

These differences are attributed to:

  ● Body size and muscle mass:Males generally have larger bodies and more muscle mass, leading to
    higher hemoglobin levels.
  ● Sex hormones:Testosterone and estrogen influence hemoglobin production, with testosterone
    stimulating erythropoiesis.

3. Pregnancy-Related Variations

Hemoglobin levels decrease during pregnancy:

  ● First trimester: Hemoglobin levels may drop due to increased blood volume.
  ● Second and third trimesters: Hemoglobin levels continue to decrease due to changes in iron
    metabolism and increased fetal demands.

4. Altitude-Related Variations

People living at high altitudes may have higher hemoglobin levels:

  ● High-altitude adaptation: The body compensates for lower oxygen levels by increasing
    erythropoiesis, leading to higher hemoglobin levels.
  ● Acclimatization:Visitors to high-altitude areas may experience temporary increases in hemoglobin
    levels as their bodies adapt.

5. Ethnicity-Related Variations

Some ethnic groups may have different hemoglobin ranges due to genetic variations:

  ● African descent: Sickle cell trait and other hemoglobinopathies are more prevalent, affecting
    hemoglobin levels.

  ● Mediterranean descent: Thalassemia and other genetic disorders may influence hemoglobin levels.

Conclusion:
The variations in hemoglobin levels are driven by physiological needs, hormonal influences, and
environmental factors. It's important to consider these contexts when interpreting hemoglobin levels to
diagnose or manage health conditions.

1. What is villi? Villi are small, finger-like projections lining the small intestine that
   increase the surface area for absorption. They contain blood vessels and lymphatics
   (lacteals) to transport nutrients absorbed from digested food.
2. Types of cells in the heart The heart contains several types of cells, including
   cardiomyocytes (contractile cells), pacemaker cells (e.g., sinoatrial node cells),
   endothelial cells (lining blood vessels), and fibroblasts (providing structural support).
3. Intestinal lumen absorption and secretion (3) o Absorption: Nutrients like
   glucose, amino acids, and fatty acids are absorbed. o           Secretion: Mucus and
   digestive enzymes are secreted. o       Electrolyte balance: Ions like Na+ and Cl- are
   absorbed or secreted to maintain balance.
4. Peptide and amine hormones Peptide hormones (e.g., insulin) are composed of
   amino acid chains and act on cell surface receptors. Amine hormones (e.g.,
   adrenaline) are derived from amino acids like tyrosine and also bind to surface
   receptors to exert their effects.
5. Hypercapnia. How animals respond to it? (9) Hypercapnia, elevated CO2 levels in
   the blood, triggers an increase in respiratory rate and depth to expel excess CO2.
   Animals may also increase blood flow to tissues and adjust bicarbonate levels to
   maintain pH balance.
6. Alimentary canal The alimentary canal, or gastrointestinal tract, is a continuous tube
   from the mouth to the anus, including the mouth, esophagus, stomach, intestines, and
   anus, responsible for digestion and nutrient absorption.

7. P wave and P-R or R-T wave interval (12) o                P wave: Represents atrial
    depolarization. o         P-R interval: Time from the start of atrial depolarization to the
    start of ventricular depolarization. o R-T interval: Represents the duration of
    ventricular depolarization and repolarization.
8. Triads in skeletal muscles Triads consist of a T-tubule flanked by two terminal
    cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, facilitating the transmission of action

Phases of a Muscle Twitch (2 Marks)

A muscle twitch consists of three distinct phases:

   1. Latent Period:
      This is the initial delay after the stimulus is applied but before contraction begins (usually
      less than 5 milliseconds). During this time, the action potential travels along the
      sarcolemma and triggers calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum.

   2. Contraction Phase:
      In this phase, the muscle fibers actively shorten as actin and myosin filaments interact via
      cross-bridge cycling. The tension increases and the muscle produces force.
   3. Relaxation Phase:
      Calcium ions are actively pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Cross-bridges
      detach, tension declines, and the muscle returns to its resting state.

Summation and Tetanus Due to Increased Stimulation Frequency (3 Marks)

When a muscle fiber is stimulated before it has completely relaxed from a previous twitch, the
new stimulus adds to the force of the first—this is known as temporal summation or wave
summation. The increased frequency allows calcium ions to accumulate in the sarcoplasm,
resulting in a stronger contraction because the muscle cannot fully relax.

If the stimulation becomes frequent enough (i.e., multiple stimuli delivered at short intervals),
the individual twitches fuse into one continuous contraction called tetanus.

There are two types:

   •   Incomplete (Unfused) Tetanus: Muscle exhibits brief periods of partial relaxation
       between contractions.
   •   Complete (Fused) Tetanus: No relaxation occurs; a smooth, sustained contraction is
       maintained.

In tetanus, calcium reuptake is overwhelmed, and cross-bridge cycling continues uninterrupted,
leading to a maximum, steady tension. This physiological mechanism ensures smooth body
movements rather than jerky twitching.

   o Drag

   ❖ Conformers

internal conditions
   ❖ Types

   o Osmoconformers
   o Oxyconformers
   o Thermoconformers

   3)    Define Facilitated Diffusion.
Passive diffusion through the membrane down the conc. Gradient with the help of
transport proteins. • It is a passive process, not requiring energy in the form of ATP.
   4)    Antiporter
Antiporters are coupled transporters that transfer two solutes in opposite directions.
   5)    Action Potentials & Importance

   ❖ Definition

• Action potentials are the type of signals that neurons use to send information over
long distances. • Actions potentials are large but brief changes in membrane potential
that are propagated along axons without decrement.
  ❖ Importance of Action Potentials
• APs are responsible for every sensation, every memory, every thought — indeed every
impulse. • They control:
   o Effector responses
   o Activation of voltage-gated ion channels
   o Muscle contraction
   o Exocytosis

  6)    How action potential is generated?

  ❖ Stimulation
• When a stimulus is received at axon hillock, it causes some voltage-gated Na+
channels to open in the neuronal membrane. • Resultantly Na+ start to diffuse in. •
This results in a local depolarization due to increase in the Vm(voltage across the
neural membrane).• A depolarization in the range of -55 to -30 mV is the threshold that
triggers an AP. • If the intensity of stimulus is less, it causes a subthreshold
depolarization that fails to generate an AP.

  ❖ Neurofibrils
• Delicate threads running from cell body into the axon and dendrites.
  ❖ Neurofibrils— Functions
• Give support and shape to the neuron. • Transport substances from cell body to the
distal cell processes.
  8)    Synapses
• Junctions between axon terminals of one neuron and the dendrites of another
neuron. • transmission of signals takes place.
  ❖ Types of Synapses

  1) Electrical synapses
  2) Chemical synapses

• Neurotransmitters are generally released in tiny packets called quanta. • Each
quantum may consist of about 2000 to 10,000 molecules of transmitter molecules.

• A myosin molecule consists of two identical heavy chains. • These chains are coiled
together to form a long tail. • Myosin also has two globular heads, made from two
heavy chains and three or four calcium-binding light chains. • The heads form cross
bridges between the thick and the thin myofilaments during contraction.

Cross bridges are formed when actin (A) and myosin (M) bind and form a stable
complex actomyosin (AM).
        A + M = AM
• This happens in the absence of ATP.
Cross-bridges b/w myosin heads & actin pull the thin filament toward the center of
sarcomere. • The force for pulling is produced by the partial rotation of myosin heads
  11) Function of Myosin
Myosin is a protein found in muscles that plays a crucial role in muscle contraction. It
forms cross-bridges with actin filaments, allowing them to slide past each other. This
sliding action shortens the muscle fibers, resulting in muscle contraction. Myosin acts
like a motor, using ATP as an energy source to generate the force needed for muscle
movement.

• After death, human and other animal’s bodies gradually become rigid. • This
condition is called rigor mortis. • This rigidity happens because ATP’s are not available
in dead body for detachment of actin and myosin, so muscles cannot relax.

Ach is excitatory at the neuromuscular junctions • It opens channels that allow Na+ to
flow in and K+ to flow out.

neurotransmitter. • ACh binds to receptors (ligand-gated ion channels) in postsynaptic
muscle fibers. • Opening of these channels causes movement of sodium (Na+) and
potassium (K+) ions.
  14) Parathormone (PTH)?
It is secreted by parathyroid gland. Increases blood Ca2+ levels; decreases blood
phosphate level
  15) How steroid hormone synthesized?
• Steroid hormones are synthesized from cholesterol. • They consist of four fused
carbon rings including three cyclohexyl rings and one cyclopentyl ring combined into a
single structure.
• Examples: hormones of adrenal cortex (cortisol and aldosterone) hormones of
ovaries (estrogen and progesterone) and hormone of testes (testosterone).

  ❖ Homeostasis—Definition

• To keep internal fluctuations in a narrow range. • The ability to protect internal
environment from the harms of fluctuations in external environment. • Homeostasis
does not mean to keep a fixed internal environment.
   ❖ Homeostasis—Examples

   o    Homeostatic regulation of water
   o    Homeostatic regulation of temperature
   o    Regulation of pH
   o    Regulation of glucose concentration
   o    Regulation of osmotic pressure
   o    Regulation of oxygen level
   o    Regulation of ion conc.

   2)     Describe Feedback Control System & its Types.

   ❖ Feedback Control Systems Definition
• Mechanism of self-regulation of Biological processes.

﻿CHAPTER-1	GENERAL THEMES IN PHYSIOLOGY
TOPIC 1		THE SPECTRUM OF STUDY OF PHYSIOLOGY
Physiology—Definition
Animal Physiology deals with the study of functions of the tissues, organs and organ systems of animals.
The ultimate goal of the study of physiology is to understand the mechanisms that operate in animals at all levels, in physical and chemical terms.
Physiological Mechanisms Obey Laws of Physics and Chemistry:
The knowledge of Physiology is firmly rooted in the laws and concepts of physics and chemistry. Following are the examples of some physical and chemical laws and concepts that relate to various physiological processes:
    • Ohm’s Law—applies to blood flow and pressure; ionic current; capacitance of membranes.
    • Boyle’s Law and the Ideal Gas Law—apply to respiration.
    • Law of Gravity—applies to blood flow.
    • Concepts of kinetic and potential energy—apply to muscle contraction; chest movements during inhalation and exhalation.
    • Concepts of Inertia, momentum, velocity and drag—apply to animal locomotion.
These are just a few examples. Many more physical and chemical laws and concepts are used to explain various physiological phenomena.
Curiosity underlies the learning of Physiology
Underlying all studies of animal physiology is the curiosity (desire to know) about how animals and their systems work. e.g.
    • How can a Hummingbird’s heart beat 20 times a second during hovering flight?
    • How do insects see in the ultraviolet spectrum?
    • How do kangaroo rats survive in the desert with no access to drinking water?
Such questions fuel the curiosity of animal physiologists and there is no bound to this curiosity. The more we know, the more we realize how little we know about physiological systems of animals.
From Animal Physiology to Human Physiology
Study of animal physiology has provided an insight into the physiological processes of humans. The human species shares the same fundamental biological processes with all other animal species and has a linked evolutionary history.
To illustrate this relationship let’s give few examples:
    • The heart beat in the human body results from the same physiological mechanisms that underlie heart function in fishes, frogs, snakes, birds, or apes.
    • Similarly, the molecular events that produce an electrical nerve impulse in the human brain are fundamentally the same as those that produce an impulse in the nerves of a squid, crab or rat.
For these reasons, the study of animal physiology has made innumerable contributions to understanding human physiology. In fact, most of what we have learned about the functions of human cells, tissues, and organs was known first through the study of various species of vertebrate and invertebrate animals.
While animal physiology lays the foundation of human physiology, the human physiology is the foundation of scientific medical practice. Understanding of the functioning and malfunctioning of living tissues provides the foundation for developing effective, scientifically sound treatment for human diseases.
In the modern times, animal physiology has contributed through new techniques for generating unique animal models for specific human diseases (e.g., diabetic mice, congenitally fat rats, zebra fish embryos with heart defects). These models allow a wide range of experiments that provide the insights into the underlying physiological processes of such diseases and defects.

Our major goals of study of animal physiology are to:
    • explore the physiological processes that are basic to all animal groups
    • show how they have been shaped by selective forces during evolution
Comparing and contrasting how different organisms have adapted to survive similar environmental challenges provides useful insights about the patterns of physiological evolution and the adaptive value of physiological processes.
Central themes in animal physiology:
As we study animal physiology and physiological adaptations, we notice several basic themes, repeatedly emerging.
We shall briefly discuss five major themes here, i.e.
    (i) Structure-function relationships
    (ii) Adaptation, Acclimatization and Acclimation
    (iii) Principle of homeostasis
    (iv) Feedback control systems
    (v) Conformity and Regulation

One of the central principles of animal physiology is that “function is based on structure”.
In other words, in living organisms, structural design is matched to functional demands.
In very simple manner we can say that the way something is arranged enables it to play its role and fulfill its job, within an organism.
Such structure-function relationships arise through evolution and natural selection.
Example:
Let’s illustrate this with a comprehensive example:
    • A frog leaps for a prey. It contracts the powerful skeletal muscles attached to the bones of its limbs.
    • As the prey is swallowed, it reaches the stomach where the smooth muscles grind and mix the food contents.
    • After digestion, the nutrients are absorbed into the blood. The blood flows due to the beating of cardiac muscles of the heart.
Throughout this process in frog’s body, three structurally distinct forms of muscles carry out three distinct functions.
Thus our basic point is elaborated:
    • The skeletal muscles are evolved and adapted for movement of the bones.
    • The smooth muscles of digestive tract are adapted for such contractions that help grinding and mixing the food materials.
    • Cardiac muscles are specialized to pump and circulate blood throughout the body.
Structure-Function Relationships are demonstrated at all levels of biological organization:
The structure-function relationships are not restricted only to the muscles but are found in every tissue of an animal’s body.
And more correctly speaking, these relationships are demonstrated at all levels of biological organization down to the molecular and atomic levels.
